Contents
Cold Start: Reversing the App First wall: two open ports The grind, compressed Free Ride: Full Control The dog shouts its name Hijack: token hand-delivered Cloud key + direct link Wall: the bashrunner whitelist Everything we tried Breakthrough: composing root seccomp, byte by byte The 150-word blacklist The chain Loot: firmware & a dead end Findings / fixes / timeline
Reverse Engineering · Featured

Driving Off With a ¥10,000 Robot Dog:
Zero-Credential Takeover to root on the Unitree GO2

A
[Author] · Sep 2026 · 40 min read · Series: GO2 (1/3)

No account. No password. Never paired over Bluetooth. Just on the same WiFi, we drove a GO2 away — walked it, ran it, made it dance, and switched off its obstacle avoidance and lights for good measure. Looking back after we had root, the hardest part wasn't any of the fancy stuff later. It was the beginning: this thing didn't seem to have a single door to walk through. Also worth noting: the dog costs about ¥10,000 — more than the second-hand laptop and old phone we attacked it with, combined.

0
credentials needed for the whole chain
31
DDS topic classes wide open once the DataChannel is up
2
"individually safe" components that compose into root RCE
2d/2w
App reversing: 2 days · zero-to-root: 2 weeks (AI-driven)
Authorization & disclosure: All testing was performed on the author's own devices and accounts. Findings were reported to Unitree's security team (security.unitree.com, timeline at the end). Key material is redacted per vendor rotation status. PoCs are read-only verification builds.
···

Cold Start: Reversing the App

Honestly, I didn't plan to reverse the app at first. Anyone in this line of work starts with a port scan — maybe there's a Telnet with a weak password or some debug port left open. What GO2 gave me was the cleanest scan result I've seen in years:

# nmap -sV, full range, all 65535 ports
PORT     STATE  SERVICE
9991/tcp open   # signaling (con_notify) — wants a key, unusable directly
8081/tcp open   # legacy signaling (offer) — same story
# That's it. Two ports. Nothing directly exploitable.

Every robot I've looked at before had something on the port surface — a debug interface, an unauthenticated admin page, some mystery service listening wide open. GO2 had nothing. Ports 9991 and 8081 were alive but wanted keys and answered nothing. I spent most of that afternoon re-scanning the same subnet with different tools and rates, as if one more pass might embarrass some port into opening up. It didn't. This was probably the first time in this kind of research that I felt properly stuck — not "hard," just no door.

No door means one remaining path: follow the official app. GO2's app (com.unitree.doggo2, v2.0.0) is where all control traffic flows — discovery, signaling, crypto, DDS calls, everything passes through it. Unitree publishes no protocol docs, and their GitHub SDK only covers motion control. So there was no choice left but to take the app apart.

A disclosure up front: this "taking apart" wasn't me reading smali line by line. An AI agent did the work — jadx decompilation, runtime dexdump, class graphs, string cross-referencing — while I asked questions and judged which of its conclusions were worth chasing. Part 3 of this series goes deep on that (including its mistakes). For now, just know this: every "we found" below really means "it found, and I verified."

The efficiency gap is real. Protocol recovery at this scale — thousands of obfuscated classes — takes a human weeks. The AI finished the app reversing in two days. But don't get the wrong idea: zero credentials to root still took two weeks. AI lets you go down wrong paths faster. The last step still costs the dumb, patient work.

The grind, compressed

The hard part of recovering a private protocol isn't the crypto — it's that out of thousands of classes, you can't tell which ones are actually alive. doggo2 is a commercially-obfuscated React Native hybrid, and only a small fraction of its classes touch the device. Those two days boiled down to one loop: drag every "protocol-looking" class into a runtime check, then throw it away. The AI, to its credit, doesn't get bored:

The protocol that finally emerged has four classes at its core:

  • UdpManager — UDP multicast discovery: broadcasts device SN and IP in cleartext
  • RtcBridgeHelper — WebRTC signaling and RTC_Start credential injection
  • RSAUtil / AESUtil — the hybrid handshake: RSA-wrapped AES session keys

With the protocol assembled, the weakness showed itself: discovery trusts you purely on SN match. Nobody asks who you are.

Free Ride: From Cleartext Multicast to Full Control

The dog shouts its name across the WiFi

GO2's discovery protocol (231.1.1.1:10134) is cleartext JSON containing {sn, ip}. Anyone on the same network hears it — the SN is no secret; the dog re-announces it every two seconds. That first night I did nothing except leave tcpdump running and watch it shout, like a golden retriever announcing its home address on a timer:

# multicast 231.1.1.1:10134, cleartext JSON, ~every 2s
{"name": "unitree_dapengche", "sn": "B42D1000QXXXXXXXX", "ip": "192.168.8.154", ...}

And what does the app do when it receives one of these? Decompiling UdpManager.handleReceivedMessage answers that in one line: it checks whether map.get("sn") matches the SN it's looking for — match means trust, and trust means follow whatever IP is in the packet. No signature. No timestamp. No replay protection of any kind.

Web folks will recognize the feeling: it's like opening a login page and finding the password field's type is text. On its own it's "just" an info leak — but it bootstraps everything after: the target's SN and current IP, delivered for free, passively.

Signaling hijack: the app hand-delivers its token

So forging a discovery response is all it takes: SN set to the dog's, IP set to ours. The app's cache got overwritten, and it promptly connected to our fake :9991 signaling server.

Then comes the most absurd part of the whole story. The app and the signaling server do an RSA-wrapped AES hybrid handshake, with AES-GCM for everything after — the crypto is fine. But once connected to our server, mid-handshake, the app sent over its accessToken as an ordinary business field.

Read that again, because the first time through it doesn't look right: the crypto is fine; the problem is the credential being handed, inside the encrypted channel, to a peer whose identity was never verified. It's like putting your money in the best safe on the market, then personally handing it to a stall with a handwritten "official safe deposit point" sign taped to it.

Cloud key + a direct line to the dog

With the accessToken we called the cloud REST API and pulled the device's handshake key (dev_key). One more handshake with the real dog using that key, and the DataChannel was up.

When the channel came up, I expected a "remote control" button set — forward, backward, a few tricks. What I counted instead was 31 classes of DDS topics, all readable and writable. This is no longer an app-level capability — it's the robot's internal bus, handed over wholesale. The app is just another user of that bus. The bridge has no api_id allowlist at all: whoever can establish a channel is standing inside the bus. Here's the full registration list the bridge logs at startup, extracted line by line from the robot's own webrtc_bridge log:

# DDS topics the bridge forwards (production log evidence, webrtc_bridge.LOG)

# —— Motion & posture ——
rt/api/sport/request             # motion control: gait / speed / FSM switching
rt/wirelesscontroller            # raw joystick commands (incl. hot-key actions)
rt/api/motion_switcher/request   # work-mode switching

# —— Execution & scripts ——
rt/api/bashrunner/request        # whitelisted script exec as root (next chapter's star)
rt/api/basic_demarcate/request   # motor/IMU calibration & power control
rt/servicestateactivate          # service-level activation
rt/selftest                      # self-test trigger

# —— Voice & sensing ——
rt/api/voice/request             # TTS / volume
rt/api/audiohub/request          # audio library upload / play / delete
rt/api/videohub/request          # video & image capture
rt/arm_service_inbound           # custom action file sync
rt/api/action_store/request      # action library management

# —— State & config ——
rt/api/robot_state/request       # service start/stop (force switch)
rt/api/config/request            # config read/write
rt/api/robot_type_service/request# model info / variant files
rt/api/rm_con/request            # remote-connection management
rt/log_system_inbound            # log system
rt/videohub/inner                # video internal channel
rt/rtc/state · rt/rtc_status     # RTC session state

# —— Telemetry (read-back side) ——
rt/lf/bmsstate · rt/lf/lowstate · rt/lf/sportmodestate ...  # battery / motor / posture

# 31 classes total: write access to motion, scripts, calibration, config, A/V

Wall: The bashrunner Whitelist Stopped the First RCE

Once the dog obeys, the next thing you want is a shell. One topic in that list looked especially juicy: rt/api/bashrunner/request — a root-running service that executes whatever {"script": "xxx"} you send it. In pentest terms that's basically a "welcome" mat on the door. Looked free.

It wasn't. There's a whitelist:

# bashrunner.py (on the robot, running as root)
command_execution_dir = current_dir + '/command_execution'
command_execution_list = os.listdir(command_execution_dir)   # snapshotted once at startup

if args[0] in command_execution_list:                     # filename must be in the list
    cmd = ["sh", command_execution_dir + '/' + args[0]]
    subprocess.run(cmd, ...)

Everything we tried

Security write-ups rarely cover the failed attempts, but getting stuck is the normal state of this work. Bottom line first: we were stopped by an os.listdir(). A function a Python beginner writes in their first hour, and it blocked every injection shape we had. For the record, these are the attempts:

AttemptIdeaCause of death
argv injection"script": "get_sn.sh; id" or "get_sn.sh -c ..."args[0] in list checks the filename first; arg injection only matters if a whitelisted script parses its args — they're all single fixed commands
Filename metachars"script": "x;id" etc.Not in the listdir snapshot → silently dropped
Path traversal"script": "../../tmp/x"The list holds bare filenames; a traversal string never matches
Overwrite a listed scriptWrite a file via the DataChannel?The channel only forwards DDS topics — no file-write primitive. We didn't yet know how to land a file.

Being stopped by a listdir is a strange feeling: the directory genuinely holds a pile of .sh files that run as root, yet you can neither add a new one nor change an old one. Like an armory with a kindergarten locker padlock on the door — and then you find out the padlock actually works. RCE attempt number one: dead.

The list is read once at process start. File in the list → run; not in the list → refuse. Remember this "startup snapshot" detail — the next chapter needs it.

Breakthrough: Two "Safe" Components Compose into root

After hitting the wall I changed the question entirely: stop looking for "exec," start looking for "is there any feature that lets a user get code running on the dog." Sweeping the app's full capability surface turned up one: "custom action programming" (programming_actuator) — users write Python, the dog runs it locally.

seccomp, byte by byte: what the sandbox actually allows

Uploaded scripts run under py_script_execute_env (the PA sandbox from here on) as root, nominally boxed in by seccomp. Most people try a couple of syscalls and give up here. I pulled its entire BPF filter out of the binary and translated every rule back to plain language:

# PA sandbox seccomp whitelist (reverse-engineered from BPF, excerpt)
deny:  execve, socket(TCP)   # no spawning processes, no network
allow: openat, write, ...    # but open & write files — as root

Stop and savor this combination for a second. The design assumption was clearly "if it can't execve, what's the harm?" But openat + write with root privileges is arbitrary file overwrite — the sandbox won't let you execute anything, but it lets you rewrite anything that will eventually be executed. Like hiring a guard whose rulebook says "rule 1: nobody fires a gun; rule 2: bullets walk in and out freely."

One more gate: the 150-word keyword blacklist

The PA upload path also scans script content for keywords — os.system, subprocess, eval and friends are all on the list. But this gate looks at words, not behavior.

The bypass is honestly pedestrian: don't write the words. Use logging.Handler — a perfectly legitimate stdlib class — for the indirect execution. The uploaded script is all logging calls, file ops, and class inheritance; nothing on the wordlist matches, yet at runtime it overwrites files. logging.Handler never asked to be part of an intrusion. It just wanted to write logs in peace.

The chain: overwrite and trigger

Now assemble the three chapters. bashrunner: whitelist snapshotted at startup, filenames-only after that. PA sandbox: can't execute, but arbitrary file write as root. Each looks fine on its own — together?

In plain words: bashrunner doesn't care what's in a file, only what it's called; the PA sandbox can't run programs but can turn any file into anything. So take a name that's already on the list and swap its contents for ours — bashrunner will execute it itself. The doorman lets people in by name tag; we just put a real name tag on a stranger.

① PA sandbox: overwrite an already-whitelisted script in command_execution/ as root
   # — name unchanged, snapshot still valid; content is ours
② trigger bashrunner to run it
   Option A: physical hotkey L1+Y (factory default)
   Option B: rt/wirelesscontroller keys=2050 (remote, zero contact)
③ bashrunner runs it as root /bin/sh with no seccomp → reverse shell

Every step sidesteps the other's design assumption: no rename, no new filename needed, execution happens outside the sandbox. When id came back with uid=0(root), chapter three's frustration finally got paid off.

Loot: 528MB of Pristine Firmware, and One Proven Dead End

First thing after the root shell: pull the entire /unitree tree off the dog (528MB / 1413 files) — untouched stock rootfs, probably the first full capture of it. From here on, no more protocol guessing; you just read the implementation.

I also did a stubborn thing that afternoon: took the freshly-proven "arbitrary write → bashrunner whitelist" pattern and swept it across every Python module on GO2 — config_service traversal, audio_hub uuid naming, push_static_file... Result: nothing. GO2's stock system doesn't have high-level modules like chat_go, so the pattern doesn't apply there.

Spending an afternoon rigorously proving a path doesn't exist — security people call that "responsible negative results," your friends at dinner call it "so what did you do all day?" But this negative result matters: R1 does have chat_go. Same pattern, and over there it lands every time. That's the next post.

Confirmed findings (all closed-loop on real hardware)

Signaling server leaks accessTokenCWE-306CriticalApp sends its cloud credential to any self-claimed signaling server

Recommendations (for the vendor)

  • Sign discovery messages / add challenge-response; the signaling service must never return credentials to unverified peers
  • Add device-ownership checks to cloud key endpoints; bind tokens to devices
  • Allowlist api_ids on the DataChannel bridge; replace the bashrunner listdir whitelist with signed scripts + 0750 directory
  • Complete the openat path allowlist in the PA sandbox; replace the keyword blacklist with AST-level analysis
  • Separate physical hotkey mappings from wireless commands; disable remote triggering

What's next

Next post is about R1. Pointing the GO2 playbook at R1's firmware worked with zero changes — same MQTT token formula, same OTA version IDOR, same direct CDN download; the cloud infrastructure is shared across products. But R1's firmware tests/ directory holds a pair of AWS credentials that made me double-check my own eyes... The post after that: R1's four RCE chains, and the arn:aws:iam::380729983040:root living in its firmware.

No robot dogs were harmed in the process (it honestly seemed to be having fun).

Driving Off With a ¥10,000 Robot Dog:
Zero-Credential Takeover to root on the Unitree GO2

A
[Author] · Sep 2026 · 40 min read · Series: GO2 (1/3)

No account. No password. Never paired over Bluetooth. Just on the same WiFi, we drove a GO2 away — walked it, ran it, made it dance, and switched off its obstacle avoidance and lights for good measure. Looking back after we had root, the hardest part wasn't any of the fancy stuff later. It was the beginning: this thing didn't seem to have a single door to walk through. Also worth noting: the dog costs about ¥10,000 — more than the second-hand laptop and old phone we attacked it with, combined.

0
credentials needed for the whole chain
31

"individually safe" components that compose into root RCE
2d/2w
App reversing: 2 days · zero-to-root: 2 weeks (AI-driven)
Authorization & disclosure: All testing was performed on the author's own devices and accounts. Findings were reported to Unitree's security team (security.unitree.com, timeline at the end). Key material is redacted per vendor rotation status. PoCs are read-only verification builds.
···

Cold Start: Reversing the App

Honestly, I didn't plan to reverse the app at first. Anyone in this line of work starts with a port scan — maybe there's a Telnet with a weak password or some debug port left open. What GO2 gave me was the cleanest scan result I've seen in years:

# nmap -sV, full range, all 65535 ports
PORT     STATE  SERVICE
9991/tcp open   # signaling (con_notify) — wants a key, unusable directly
8081/tcp open   # legacy signaling (offer) — same story
# That's it. Two ports. Nothing directly exploitable.

Every robot I've looked at before had something on the port surface — a debug interface, an unauthenticated admin page, some mystery service listening wide open. GO2 had nothing. Ports 9991 and 8081 were alive but wanted keys and answered nothing. I spent most of that afternoon re-scanning the same subnet with different tools and rates, as if one more pass might embarrass some port into opening up. It didn't. This was probably the first time in this kind of research that I felt properly stuck — not "hard," just no door.

No door means one remaining path: follow the official app. GO2's app (com.unitree.doggo2, v2.0.0) is where all control traffic flows — discovery, signaling, crypto, DDS calls, everything passes through it. Unitree publishes no protocol docs, and their GitHub SDK only covers motion control. So there was no choice left but to take the app apart.

A disclosure up front: this "taking apart" wasn't me reading smali line by line. An AI agent did the work — jadx decompilation, runtime dexdump, class graphs, string cross-referencing — while I asked questions and judged which of its conclusions were worth chasing. Part 3 of this series goes deep on that (including its mistakes). For now, just know this: every "we found" below really means "it found, and I verified."

The efficiency gap is real. Protocol recovery at this scale — thousands of obfuscated classes — takes a human weeks. The AI finished the app reversing in two days. But don't get the wrong idea: zero credentials to root still took two weeks. AI lets you go down wrong paths faster. The last step still costs the dumb, patient work.

The grind, compressed

The hard part of recovering a private protocol isn't the crypto — it's that out of thousands of classes, you can't tell which ones are actually alive. doggo2 is a commercially-obfuscated React Native hybrid, and only a small fraction of its classes touch the device. Those two days boiled down to one loop: drag every "protocol-looking" class into a runtime check, then throw it away. The AI, to its credit, doesn't get bored:

The protocol that finally emerged has four classes at its core:

  • UdpManager — UDP multicast discovery: broadcasts device SN and IP in cleartext
  • RtcBridgeHelper — WebRTC signaling and RTC_Start credential injection
  • RSAUtil / AESUtil — the hybrid handshake: RSA-wrapped AES session keys

With the protocol assembled, the weakness showed itself: discovery trusts you purely on SN match. Nobody asks who you are.

Free Ride: From Cleartext Multicast to Full Control

The dog shouts its name across the WiFi

GO2's discovery protocol (231.1.1.1:10134) is cleartext JSON containing {sn, ip}. Anyone on the same network hears it — the SN is no secret; the dog re-announces it every two seconds. That first night I did nothing except leave tcpdump running and watch it shout, like a golden retriever announcing its home address on a timer:

# multicast 231.1.1.1:10134, cleartext JSON, ~every 2s
{"name": "unitree_dapengche", "sn": "B42D1000QXXXXXXXX", "ip": "192.168.8.154", ...}

And what does the app do when it receives one of these? Decompiling UdpManager.handleReceivedMessage answers that in one line: it checks whether map.get("sn") matches the SN it's looking for — match means trust, and trust means follow whatever IP is in the packet. No signature. No timestamp. No replay protection of any kind.

Web folks will recognize the feeling: it's like opening a login page and finding the password field's type is text. On its own it's "just" an info leak — but it bootstraps everything after: the target's SN and current IP, delivered for free, passively.

Signaling hijack: the app hand-delivers its token

So forging a discovery response is all it takes: SN set to the dog's, IP set to ours. The app's cache got overwritten, and it promptly connected to our fake :9991 signaling server.

Then comes the most absurd part of the whole story. The app and the signaling server do an RSA-wrapped AES hybrid handshake, with AES-GCM for everything after — the crypto is fine. But once connected to our server, mid-handshake, the app sent over its accessToken as an ordinary business field.

Read that again, because the first time through it doesn't look right: the crypto is fine; the problem is the credential being handed, inside the encrypted channel, to a peer whose identity was never verified. It's like putting your money in the best safe on the market, then personally handing it to a stall with a handwritten "official safe deposit point" sign taped to it.

Cloud key + a direct line to the dog

With the accessToken we called the cloud REST API and pulled the device's handshake key (dev_key). One more handshake with the real dog using that key, and the DataChannel was up.

When the channel came up, I expected a "remote control" button set — forward, backward, a few tricks. What I counted instead was 31 classes of DDS topics, all readable and writable. This is no longer an app-level capability — it's the robot's internal bus, handed over wholesale. The app is just another user of that bus. The bridge has no api_id allowlist at all: whoever can establish a channel is standing inside the bus. Here's the full registration list the bridge logs at startup, extracted line by line from the robot's own webrtc_bridge log:

# DDS topics the bridge forwards (production log evidence, webrtc_bridge.LOG)

# —— Motion & posture ——
rt/api/sport/request             # motion control: gait / speed / FSM switching
rt/wirelesscontroller            # raw joystick commands (incl. hot-key actions)
rt/api/motion_switcher/request   # work-mode switching

# —— Execution & scripts ——
rt/api/bashrunner/request        # whitelisted script exec as root (next chapter's star)
rt/api/basic_demarcate/request   # motor/IMU calibration & power control
rt/servicestateactivate          # service-level activation
rt/selftest                      # self-test trigger

# —— Voice & sensing ——
rt/api/voice/request             # TTS / volume
rt/api/audiohub/request          # audio library upload / play / delete
rt/api/videohub/request          # video & image capture
rt/arm_service_inbound           # custom action file sync
rt/api/action_store/request      # action library management

# —— State & config ——
rt/api/robot_state/request       # service start/stop (force switch)
rt/api/config/request            # config read/write
rt/api/robot_type_service/request# model info / variant files
rt/api/rm_con/request            # remote-connection management
rt/log_system_inbound            # log system
rt/videohub/inner                # video internal channel
rt/rtc/state · rt/rtc_status     # RTC session state

# —— Telemetry (read-back side) ——
rt/lf/bmsstate · rt/lf/lowstate · rt/lf/sportmodestate ...  # battery / motor / posture

# 31 classes total: write access to motion, scripts, calibration, config, A/V

Wall: The bashrunner Whitelist Stopped the First RCE

Once the dog obeys, the next thing you want is a shell. One topic in that list looked especially juicy: rt/api/bashrunner/request — a root-running service that executes whatever {"script": "xxx"} you send it. In pentest terms that's basically a "welcome" mat on the door. Looked free.

It wasn't. There's a whitelist:

# bashrunner.py (on the robot, running as root)
command_execution_dir = current_dir + '/command_execution'
command_execution_list = os.listdir(command_execution_dir)   # snapshotted once at startup

if args[0] in command_execution_list:                     # filename must be in the list
    cmd = ["sh", command_execution_dir + '/' + args[0]]
    subprocess.run(cmd, ...)

Everything we tried

Security write-ups rarely cover the failed attempts, but getting stuck is the normal state of this work. Bottom line first: we were stopped by an os.listdir(). A function a Python beginner writes in their first hour, and it blocked every injection shape we had. For the record, these are the attempts:

AttemptIdeaCause of death
argv injection"script": "get_sn.sh; id" or "get_sn.sh -c ..."args[0] in list checks the filename first; arg injection only matters if a whitelisted script parses its args — they're all single fixed commands
Filename metachars"script": "x;id" etc.Not in the listdir snapshot → silently dropped
Path traversal"script": "../../tmp/x"The list holds bare filenames; a traversal string never matches
Overwrite a listed scriptWrite a file via the DataChannel?The channel only forwards DDS topics — no file-write primitive. We didn't yet know how to land a file.

Being stopped by a listdir is a strange feeling: the directory genuinely holds a pile of .sh files that run as root, yet you can neither add a new one nor change an old one. Like an armory with a kindergarten locker padlock on the door — and then you find out the padlock actually works. RCE attempt number one: dead.

The list is read once at process start. File in the list → run; not in the list → refuse. Remember this "startup snapshot" detail — the next chapter needs it.

Breakthrough: Two "Safe" Components Compose into root

After hitting the wall I changed the question entirely: stop looking for "exec," start looking for "is there any feature that lets a user get code running on the dog." Sweeping the app's full capability surface turned up one: "custom action programming" (programming_actuator) — users write Python, the dog runs it locally.

seccomp, byte by byte: what the sandbox actually allows

Uploaded scripts run under py_script_execute_env (the PA sandbox from here on) as root, nominally boxed in by seccomp. Most people try a couple of syscalls and give up here. I pulled its entire BPF filter out of the binary and translated every rule back to plain language:

# PA sandbox seccomp whitelist (reverse-engineered from BPF, excerpt)
deny:  execve, socket(TCP)   # no spawning processes, no network
allow: openat, write, ...    # but open & write files — as root

Stop and savor this combination for a second. The design assumption was clearly "if it can't execve, what's the harm?" But openat + write with root privileges is arbitrary file overwrite — the sandbox won't let you execute anything, but it lets you rewrite anything that will eventually be executed. Like hiring a guard whose rulebook says "rule 1: nobody fires a gun; rule 2: bullets walk in and out freely."

One more gate: the 150-word keyword blacklist

The PA upload path also scans script content for keywords — os.system, subprocess, eval and friends are all on the list. But this gate looks at words, not behavior.

The bypass is honestly pedestrian: don't write the words. Use logging.Handler — a perfectly legitimate stdlib class — for the indirect execution. The uploaded script is all logging calls, file ops, and class inheritance; nothing on the wordlist matches, yet at runtime it overwrites files. logging.Handler never asked to be part of an intrusion. It just wanted to write logs in peace.

The chain: overwrite and trigger

Now assemble the three chapters. bashrunner: whitelist snapshotted at startup, filenames-only after that. PA sandbox: can't execute, but arbitrary file write as root. Each looks fine on its own — together?

In plain words: bashrunner doesn't care what's in a file, only what it's called; the PA sandbox can't run programs but can turn any file into anything. So take a name that's already on the list and swap its contents for ours — bashrunner will execute it itself. The doorman lets people in by name tag; we just put a real name tag on a stranger.

① PA sandbox: overwrite an already-whitelisted script in command_execution/ as root
   # — name unchanged, snapshot still valid; content is ours
② trigger bashrunner to run it
   Option A: physical hotkey L1+Y (factory default)
   Option B: rt/wirelesscontroller keys=2050 (remote, zero contact)
③ bashrunner runs it as root /bin/sh with no seccomp → reverse shell

Every step sidesteps the other's design assumption: no rename, no new filename needed, execution happens outside the sandbox. When id came back with uid=0(root), chapter three's frustration finally got paid off.

Loot: 528MB of Pristine Firmware, and One Proven Dead End

First thing after the root shell: pull the entire /unitree tree off the dog (528MB / 1413 files) — untouched stock rootfs, probably the first full capture of it. From here on, no more protocol guessing; you just read the implementation.

I also did a stubborn thing that afternoon: took the freshly-proven "arbitrary write → bashrunner whitelist" pattern and swept it across every Python module on GO2 — config_service traversal, audio_hub uuid naming, push_static_file... Result: nothing. GO2's stock system doesn't have high-level modules like chat_go, so the pattern doesn't apply there.

Spending an afternoon rigorously proving a path doesn't exist — security people call that "responsible negative results," your friends at dinner call it "so what did you do all day?" But this negative result matters: R1 does have chat_go. Same pattern, and over there it lands every time. That's the next post.

Findings, Fixes, and Disclosure Timeline

Confirmed findings (all closed-loop on real hardware)

FindingCWESeverityOne-liner
Cleartext multicast discovery + SN-as-trustCWE-345HighDiscovery is unauthenticated; forged responses hijack signaling
Signaling server leaks accessTokenCWE-306CriticalApp sends its cloud credential to any self-claimed signaling server
Cloud dev_key readable without ownership checkCWE-639CriticalAny account token reads any bound device's handshake key
DataChannel → all 31 DDS topic classesCWE-306CriticalNo api_id allowlist; internal bus fully open
PA sandbox seccomp allows openat/writeCWE-693CriticalArbitrary file write as root
bashrunner whitelist bypass via overwriteCWE-78CriticalSnapshot list + writable dir = composed root
keys=2050 remote hotkey triggerCWE-306HighPhysical hotkey actions remotely triggerable, zero contact

Recommendations (for the vendor)

  • Sign discovery messages / add challenge-response; the signaling service must never return credentials to unverified peers
  • Add device-ownership checks to cloud key endpoints; bind tokens to devices
  • Allowlist api_ids on the DataChannel bridge; replace the bashrunner listdir whitelist with signed scripts + 0750 directory
  • Complete the openat path allowlist in the PA sandbox; replace the keyword blacklist with AST-level analysis
  • Separate physical hotkey mappings from wireless commands; disable remote triggering

Disclosure timeline

DateEvent
2026-07Full GO2 chain closed on hardware (zero-cred control + root RCE)
[TBD]Initial report to security.unitree.com
[TBD]Vendor acknowledgment / fix / CVE assignment
[TBD]Publication

What's next

Next post is about R1. Pointing the GO2 playbook at R1's firmware worked with zero changes — same MQTT token formula, same OTA version IDOR, same direct CDN download; the cloud infrastructure is shared across products. But R1's firmware tests/ directory holds a pair of AWS credentials that made me double-check my own eyes... The post after that: R1's four RCE chains, and the arn:aws:iam::380729983040:root living in its firmware.

Methodology note: This research was driven end-to-end by an AI agent (reversing, protocol recovery, vulnerability composition). The human author handled authorization boundaries, final judgment calls, and saying "look again" when the agent was confidently wrong. All testing was done on the author's own devices and accounts. No robot dogs were harmed in the process (it honestly seemed to be having fun).

Driving Off With a ¥10,000 Robot Dog:
Zero-Credential Takeover to root on the Unitree GO2

A
[Author] · Sep 2026 · 40 min read · Series: GO2 (1/3)

No account. No password. Never paired anything. Just sitting on the same WiFi, we drove a GO2 away — walked it, ran it, made it dance, and switched off its obstacle avoidance and lights for good measure. Looking back after root, the hardest part wasn't any of the fancy stuff later. It was the beginning: this thing genuinely appeared to have no door. Also worth a footnote: the dog costs about ¥10,000 — more than the second-hand laptop and beat-up phone we attacked it with. Combined. 🙃

App reversing 2 days · zero-to-root 2 weeks
Authorization & disclosure: Everything below was done on my own dog and my own account. Findings went to Unitree's security team first (security.unitree.com, timeline at the end). Keys are redacted where the vendor hasn't rotated them yet. PoCs are read-only verification builds.
···

Cold Start: Reversing the App

Honest confession: I didn't want to reverse the app. Reversing apps is work. Port scanning is five minutes and maybe there's a Telnet with password admin in it. So I scanned. And GO2 handed me the cleanest result I've seen in years:

# nmap -sV, full range, all 65535 ports
PORT     STATE  SERVICE
9991/tcp open   # signaling (con_notify) — wants a key, answers nothing
8081/tcp open   # legacy signaling (offer) — same
# That's it. Two ports. Nothing directly exploitable. Great.

Every robot I've looked at before had something — a debug port, an unauthenticated admin page, some mystery service with its fly down. GO2 had nothing.
